name: Vasa praevia
aliases: unprotected fetal vessels over the cervical os
unprotected fetal vessels over the cervix

clinicalPearls: Vasa praevia describes fetal blood vessels coursing through the membranes across or in close proximity to the internal cervical os, unsupported by placental tissue or the umbilical cord
Two principal types are recognised: type 1, associated with a velamentous cord insertion, and type 2, in which vessels run between the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate-lobed placenta

The danger is rupture of these unprotected vessels when the membranes rupture, causing rapid fetal exsanguination; because the blood lost is fetal, even a modest volume is life-threatening to the baby
The classic intrapartum presentation is painless vaginal bleeding at the time of membrane rupture accompanied by acute fetal heart rate abnormalities such as a sinusoidal trace or bradycardia
Antenatal diagnosis by transvaginal ultrasound with colour and pulsed-wave Doppler, demonstrating fetal-origin vessels over the os, transforms the prognosis by allowing planned delivery before labour
Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, a bilobed or succenturiate-lobed placenta, a low-lying placenta or resolved praevia, multiple pregnancy, and conception by assisted reproduction

Management of confirmed vasa praevia is planned hospital admission in the third trimester, corticosteroids for lung maturity, and elective caesarean section before the onset of labour and before the membranes rupture
When vasa praevia is unrecognised and a vessel ruptures, the priority is immediate delivery and neonatal resuscitation with volume replacement, as the newborn may require urgent transfusion
reference.pathophysiology: Normally the umbilical vessels insert centrally into the placental mass and are cushioned by Wharton's jelly, while the fetal chorionic vessels are protected by surrounding placenta. In vasa praevia this protection is lost: either the cord inserts into the membranes (velamentous insertion) with vessels traversing the membranes before reaching the placenta, or vessels bridge between separate placental lobes. When these membranous vessels overlie the internal os they lie below the presenting part and across the path of delivery, without protective Wharton's jelly, and are vulnerable both to compression by the presenting part and, critically, to laceration when the overlying membranes rupture spontaneously or artificially. Rupture opens the low-volume fetal circulation directly, so brisk fetal haemorrhage and exsanguination can occur within minutes.
additionalDifferentials: Local maternal genital tract bleeding from a cervical or vaginal lesion
A maternal rather than fetal source of intrapartum bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler to identify vessels crossing or lying near the internal os
Pulsed-wave Doppler to confirm a fetal heart rate waveform within the aberrant vessels
Assessment of cord insertion site and placental morphology, including a bilobed or succenturiate lobe, at the routine anomaly scan
Cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise such as a sinusoidal pattern or bradycardia
Bedside testing to distinguish fetal from maternal blood, such as an alkali-denaturation (Apt) or Kleihauer test, though delivery should not await results
Maternal full blood count and group-and-save or crossmatch
redFlags: Vaginal bleeding coinciding with rupture of the membranes
Sinusoidal or profoundly abnormal fetal heart rate pattern
Acute fetal bradycardia after spontaneous or artificial rupture of the membranes
Known velamentous cord insertion or succenturiate lobe presenting undiagnosed in labour
Rapidly deteriorating fetal condition with only a modest volume of fresh vaginal blood
reference.prognosis: With antenatal diagnosis and elective caesarean before labour, perinatal survival is excellent. When the diagnosis is first made after vessel rupture, perinatal mortality is high owing to the speed of fetal exsanguination.
pitfalls: Attributing intrapartum bleeding to a maternal cause and delaying delivery while fetal blood is being lost
Rupturing membranes without first palpating for pulsating vessels when vasa praevia is possible
Failing to identify a velamentous cord insertion or a succenturiate lobe on antenatal scanning
Not re-imaging a low-lying placenta or resolved praevia for associated vasa praevia
Under-preparing for immediate neonatal resuscitation and transfusion at delivery
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on vasa praevia
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Plan an elective caesarean section before the onset of labour and before membrane rupture, timed to the late preterm period to pre-empt vessel rupture
Administer antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation ahead of the scheduled preterm delivery
Undertake third-trimester surveillance with serial ultrasound and consider inpatient admission for monitoring with immediate theatre access
Avoid artificial rupture of membranes and any attempt at vaginal delivery

Treat membrane rupture accompanied by foetal heart rate abnormality or bleeding as an obstetric emergency, proceeding to immediate caesarean with neonatal resuscitation and volume and blood replacement for the exsanguinated baby
Coordinate care across obstetrics, neonatology and anaesthesia, delivering in a unit with neonatal intensive care
Ensure emergency neonatal blood transfusion is available given the risk of rapid foetal haemorrhage
